theme: The Levites and their duties, sacred service
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 3:1-4:49. Yesterday you saw the camp of the tribes. Today you read about the tribe of Levi, who were set apart to serve in the tabernacle. Notice the contrast between the Levites and the firstborn of Israel.
settingTheScene: Numbers 3 and 4 describe the Levites, the tribe of Moses and Aaron. They are not counted with the army, because their work is different: they guard and carry the tabernacle. The chapters list the three clans of Levi, Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, and assign each a duty. They also explain why the Levites belong to God. When the firstborn of Egypt died at the Passover, the firstborn of Israel were spared, and so they belonged to the LORD. God takes the Levites as a substitute for them.
observation: The sons of Aaron are named, and the death of Nadab and Abihu is recalled (3:1-4).
The Levites are given to Aaron “as a gift” to assist him (3:5-10).
“I have taken the Levites from among the people of Israel instead of every firstborn” (3:12).
The three clans of Levi camp on three sides of the tabernacle, with Moses and Aaron at the east (3:21-39).
The firstborn of Israel outnumber the Levites by 273, and each of the extra is redeemed for five shekels (3:40-51).
The Kohathites carry the holy things, but must not touch or look at them, “lest they die” (4:15, 20).
Aaron and his sons must first cover the furniture before the Kohathites come to carry it (4:5-15).
The Levites serve from age thirty to fifty (4:3, 23, 30).
interpretation:
This section teaches one of the Bible’s basic ideas: substitution. The firstborn of Israel were saved at the Passover, and they belonged to God because of it. Instead of requiring every firstborn son to serve at the sanctuary, God takes the Levites in their place. The Levites stand in for the firstborn, and when there are extra firstborn, a ransom price is paid. The principle is that a life spared must be given back to the one who spared it.

The Levites’ work is a lesson in reverence. The Kohathites carry the most holy things, but they are never allowed to touch them or look at them directly. The priests have to cover the furniture first. It is a vivid warning that God’s holiness is not casual. Even people set apart to serve him can only approach him in the way he has provided.

The text also shows the dignity of ordinary service. Much of the Levites’ work was carrying poles and curtains. It was heavy and repetitive. But Numbers describes it carefully, with each task named, because in God’s household no task is small. The people who carried the tent poles are as precisely recorded as the priests who burned the incense.

And the redemption of the extra firstborn shows how seriously God takes the ransom principle. Five shekels each is a price, a reminder that the people did not belong to themselves.

All of this prepares the reader for the greater substitution. God spared Israel’s firstborn, and then God gave his own firstborn, the only Son, as a ransom for many.
connection: Jesus is called “the firstborn of all creation” and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:15, 18). Believers are called “the assembly of the firstborn” (Hebrews 12:23). Peter says that you were “ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18-19). Paul says that you are not your own, because you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).
application:
Think about what it means to belong to God because of what he has done for you. Ask how that shapes your daily choices.

Honor those who do humble service in your church, such as people who set up, clean, or carry.

Receive the ransom with gratitude, and offer your service back to the one who redeemed you.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for the ransom of his Son, and tell him what it means that you are not your own.
Offer him your hands and your days, naming one thing specific.
Ask him to teach you to honor his holiness.
